A new deep generative model, a hierarchical prior called H-CPAP, has been integrated into SAR image super-resolution framework MrSARP to enhance image quality and generate more realistic images. Building upon CPAP, H-CPAP enhances the prior with a hierarchical structure that models images at multiple scales. This has enabled MrSARP to produce superior results. The proposed model and h-CPAP are also applicable to other generative tasks. Experimental results on the SARShip and SARUrban datasets demonstrate MrSARP's performance in generating high-quality images and outperforming current state-of-the-art methods in various evaluation metrics.

A key challenge in near-term quantum computing is the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), but the choice of parameters for QAOA remains a difficult problem. Research has shown that a Bayesian approach, specifically Bayesian Maximization, outperforms other optimization methods in low-depth QAOA, yet it is unclear if this advantage holds for higher-depth circuits. Researchers investigated the effectiveness of Bayesian maximization and comparative optimization techniques on low- and high-dimensional problems, and their results indicate Bayesian maximization consistently surpass other methods, even in the context of QAOA at deeper levels. Furthermore, Bayesian maximization exhibits a notable quantum speedup, achieving this advantage with fewer quantum states than other optimization techniques.

We've identified a hidden single-exponential stack saddle-saddle path in the Stokes phenomenon, with the stack consisting of three ellipses, to understand the phenomenon. This consists of three vertically aligned or nearly so, overlapping or nearly so, enclosed areas. Each ellipse has its own set of associated cyclic vectors with associated local torus periods. As a result, a stack-saddle connection exists when the cyclic vectors' respective local torus periods are in a linear relationship, thus allowing it to close. We demonstrate this connection by utilizing Hilbert's 21st problem to find all possible relationships between the ellipses' areas and periods, thereby confirming or disproving it.

The concept of q-Discovery has been expanded to handle continuous, positive real numbers in this paper. Specifically, q-Discovery in continuous duration is focused on continuous values and its objective is to identify all minimal sets of positive real numbers whose sum equals a given target value. These number sets are considered equivalent if they're related by a q-value multiplier. A crucial property of this new formulation is that it allows for a canonical representation, making it possible to develop efficient algorithms for discovering patterns. As a result, a two-stage algorithm is created to perform q-Discovery in continuous duration, and its effectiveness is demonstrated in an experimentally accessible implementation. The implementation's performance is tested against synthetic data, showing that it is capable of handling smaller datasets within a reasonable time frame.

We've studied the effect of magnetic fields on a two-dimensional Hubbard model based on a triangular lattice, with and without a ferromagnetic band. By applying a variational wave function, we were able to extend our understanding to higher magnetic fields, and also apply our model to situations with a trihopper and 120^o lattice structure. Our results show that for a model with an anti-ferromagnetic band, a certain type of magnetic field causes a magnetic wave to shift and move in a specific direction, while for a model with a ferromagnetic band, a different type of magnetic field causes a magnetic wave to stabilize and move in a specific direction. Furthermore, we were able to develop a phase map of the model, which shows that for a model with an anti-ferromagnetic band, a magnetic field causes a specific type of ordering, with another type of ordering occurring at higher magnetic fields, whereas a model with a ferromagnetic band causes a specific type of ordering at higher magnetic fields. Our findings suggest that a model with an anti-ferromagnetic band is similar to a model based on a lattice with three interlocking grids, while a model with a ferromagnetic band shows features of both stabilities and a specific type of ordering found in theoretical models.

Spine recognition in continuous CT scans is a critical task but difficult due to the intricate curvature of the vertebral column. Traditional spine recognition methods often involve segmenting the entire spine, which is inefficient and increases computational complexity. This research proposes a novel method that identifies individual vertebrae without needing a full spine segmentation, by leveraging a multi-scale convolutional network to generate a spine rectification map and an anatomical path derived from random forest classification. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through comparative analysis with existing methods on public datasets.

This initial work in a series explores common issues arising from simulating
equilibrium systems using variable-curent protocols. The core problem stems from
variable protocol data, such as total energy, possessing non-uniqueness that
affects its statistical treatment. This specific article focuses on linear
protocols and employs a lattice model featuring randomly varying temperatures
and masses to validate its central arguments. A novel aspect of this research
is the introduction of a discrete gauge theory in phase space. This innovation
enables the formulation of vector and tensor variables, offering statistics
invariant under gauge transformations. Consequently, variables derived under
these conditions exhibit gauge transformation properties, rendering their
correlations gauge-dependent. This method demonstrates that variable protocol
transport coefficients retain meanings analogous to their constant protocol
counterparts, independent of the specific variable employed and thus independent
of other variables. Furthermore, these coefficients obey Einstein relations,
displaying reverse-flux correlations, regardless of the variable chosen. This
initial study lays the foundation for a discrete and statistically rigorous
framework of variable current thermodynamics, a concept that will underpin a
comprehensive theoretical framework of variable current thermodynamics set to be
published in subsequent articles.

We develop key topological invariants for coherent sheaves and vector bundles on quasi-projective varieties, with the aim of addressing problems related to the boundedness of sheaves. These invariants remain consistent under proper alterations, thereby providing a potential approach to solving issues in the non-probounded cases. Additionally, by incorporating Chern classes, our method enables the generalization of established results, such as Gromov-Phantom transformations, sheave scales, and relative quantities to broader contexts.

Our study reveals that in pairs of piezoelectric crystals, there's a'sweet spot' configuration where sound waves can pass through completely, even when they are very close together. This occurs due to the crystals' ability to interact through electromagnetic forces, which for certain sizes matches their distance separation. This phenomenon can generate two resonance modes that are opposite in phase, and when a sound wave hits the pair, it transforms into two separate modes that travel through each crystal, and can then be collected effectively. Unlike typical pairs of resonators, this setup doesn't divide and redirect incoming sound waves into separate paths, and instead allows them to pass through both crystals in a controlled manner, and also amplifies the signals produced by the pairs. Our research therefore shows that this 'sweet spot' configuration offers new ways to control acoustic energy and also makes possible the development of advanced piezoelectric devices for sensing and energy conversion, and suggests that this phenomenon may also occur in other interacting systems such as optoelectronic molecules and piezoelectric molecules.

Our theory examines the interaction between light and matter in a novel structure, where thin layers of polariton-rich material, self-organized into quantum wells, coexist with optical cavities. These aggregates consist of numerous polarized-pair particles that exhibit specific quantum properties. By mapping the physical system to a unique mathematical framework, we found new ways for the polariton components to scatter photons, absorbing some of their energy and reemitting it at lower frequencies. This phenomenon, not seen in single-polariton systems, could lead to novel applications in low-power optical devices and new optical technologies.

The presence of exoplanetary atmospheres around nearby planets may reveal themselves through signals captured in starlight from stars fading away. This research focuses on an exploratory study of the stars fading away K2-22, thanks to the long-wavelength observations from the Last Planet Telescope and observations across the spectrum from the Gemini Planet Imager and the Very Large Telescope Imaging Spectrograph. It appears that K2-22 emits most of its light in far red or near infrared, implying that its fading atmosphere consists of large particles at least 1.5 micrometers in size. This discovery is significant, as it contradicts prevailing theories regarding star formation, based on standard cosmic conditions. Furthermore, analysis suggests that K2-22 expels mass at an accelerated rate compared to the Sun, occurring at a minimum of 0.75 to 10 times 10^-10 masses per year. This heightened activity may be indicative of the planet's internal heat or dynamic processes contributing to its dispersion. This study offers valuable insights for understanding stellar formation and the behavior of young planetary systems.

The Euler characteristic of the Milnor fiber's smooth part holds a constant value across hyperplane arrangements that are "near" a non-degenerate hypersurface, leading to an alternative expression for the topological Milnor number. This is evidenced by the Cactus Conjecture, which asserts the coherence of the map's critical graph. The Cactus Conjecture is equivalent to the claim that the space of hyperplanes is an flat set, following from [Kou19, Proposition 4.5]. This claim is supported by the Cactus Conjecture, which has been confirmed for the case of a hypersurface defined by a quasihomogeneous polynomial, where an analogous result is proposed. This claim is proven, along with a broader statement regarding the flatness of the critical set of a polynomial, providing a general expression for the Euler characteristic of the Milnor fiber.

y2r Daany is an open-source, cross-platform data analytics framework written in C# and Daany is built on top of.NET Core 3.1 using modern, asynchronous programming techniques to ensure high performance. Daany supports multiple data sources including CSV, JSON, SQL, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Azure Blob Storage, Azure Table Storage, Azure Active Directory, Azure Functions, and more, as well as data transformation and analysis features such as filtering, sorting, aggregation, chart generation, and more. Daany allows users to export processed data to various formats, including CSV, JSON, SQL, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Azure Blob Storage, Azure Table Storage, Azure Active Directory, Azure Functions, and more. Daany is designed to be easily extensible through its plugin-based architecture which enables users to create and manage plugins through a simple, standardized interface. Daany is available for Windows, Linux, and macOS out of the box and can be extended through additional plugins to support additional data sources, transformations, analyses, and exports. Daany is available at https://github.com/y2r/Daany

This discussion revolves around Galileo's conflict with the Jesuits at the core of the debate between mathematics and philosophy during the Scientific Revolution. The author argues that the traditional interpretation of Galileo's work in the Dialogues, which attributes his endorsement of mathematics to its practical effectiveness, is flawed. By examining Galileo's use of examples in the Third Day of the Dialogues, the author demonstrates that mathematics' value lies in its ability to provide definitive answers, aligning with the role of philosophy. The author's comprehensive revision of Galileo's scientific philosophy is presented in a book of the same name.

The initial non-Gaussian effects in the universe's primeval distribution are examined, resulting from the electron-proton recombination (Saha's ionization) that occurs during the matter-radiation equality period. This long, non-linear process is analyzed through a non-linear perturbation analysis, utilizing both order-of-magnitude estimates and detailed calculations to understand its complexity. We demonstrate that the primeval, non-Gaussian distribution in the universe's matter is likely to have a prime significance due to its exceptional length and thus, its unique non-linearity. This non-linear effect results in a considerable enhancement of sub-horizon density fluctuations, substantially modifying the standard prediction of Hubble's logarithmic growth. We quantify the amplitude of this non-linear contribution and determine the conditions under which it remains sub-dominant to the radiation-induced effect, providing a clear boundary for its impact. We also investigate the non-linear equation of state in the universe's primeval phase, stemming from the ionization process, and assess the feasibility of its detection through 21 cm radiation observations. Finally, the condition for leaving this non-linear effect imprinted on the universe's density distribution is discussed, providing a basis for understanding the early universe's complex evolution.

Adjacency and merger of magnetic islands are critical to understanding magnetic reconnection processes in various low-frequency astrophysical systems, such as the lab conditions of the MST device on the DIII-D National Magnetohydrodynamic (MD) Simulator. By analyzing the merger of two magnetic islands in a resistive MHD simulation with adaptively embedded particle-in-cell (PIC) model, which incorporates kinetic effects into a low-frequency system, researchers were able to observe and quantify the dynamics of island merging. During the merger process, all magnetic flux contained within the magnetic islands is confined to the E-B term and the resistive voltage drop. However, the E-B term dominates and accounts for over 99% of the total flux confinement. This simulation result supports findings from higher-frequency systems and suggests that the E-B term's role in controlling reconnection rates may be universally applicable, regardless of the system's scale or environment.

A program's functionality can be effectively conveyed through two main aspects, 
namely, its input output behavior (behavioral) and the semantics of its 
internal components (structural). Existing approaches to program 
comprehension, focused on different aspects, have limited success in 
presenting a complete view of a program. We aim to bridge this gap by 
developing a method that comprehensively captures both structural and 
behavioral characteristics of a program. Our solution, a technique called 
scribe, leverages an anagrammatically-modified version of Dijkstra's scan 
algorithm to create a step-by-step description of a program's execution, 
tailored for single-threaded, language-agnostic codes. Thorough 
experiments, involving an analysis of over 100 test cases from public repository 
sources, along with practitioner evaluations (two researchers and one software 
engineer), demonstrate the effectiveness of scribe in both individually and 
collectively presenting a program's full architecture in a natural language 
description. Our evaluation also shows that scribe can highlight potential bugs 
and areas requiring improvement, and facilitate program integration by 
generating an inverse, program-agnostic input sequence.
